Marketing has changed a lot in the last decade. Brands used to rely on television, print, and radio to reach customers, but now social media platforms let even small businesses reach millions of people for very little money. This shift has created new opportunities and new problems. On one hand, a local bakery can build a loyal following on Instagram without paying for a billboard. On the other hand, the sheer amount of content means attention is harder to win than ever. Companies now compete not only with their direct rivals but with every creator, meme, and video in a user's feed. Successful brands have responded by focusing on authenticity, community, and consistent posting rather than polished campaigns. They also measure everything, from click-through rates to how long people watch a video. In this essay I argue that the most important marketing skill today is not creativity alone but the ability to learn quickly from data while keeping a human voice.

As a computer science student at a university in New York, I have spent the last two years building products that real people use. The water cycle describes how water moves through the environment. Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and rivers when the sun heats it, turning into water vapor that rises into the atmosphere. As the vapor rises, it cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. When enough droplets combine, they become heavy and fall back to Earth as precipitation, which can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail. Some of this water flows over the land as runoff and collects in rivers and oceans, while some soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. Plants also release water vapor through a process called transpiration. The cycle has no real start or end, and it is powered mostly by energy from the sun. Understanding the water cycle helps scientists predict weather, manage water supplies, and study how climate change may affect droughts and floods around the world in the coming decades.

Our club had a great semester. We hosted six events, including two workshops on resume writing, a networking night with alumni, and a hackathon that drew more than forty participants. Attendance grew steadily over the semester, and many new members told us they joined because a friend brought them to an event. We also partnered with the career center for the first time, which helped us get rooms and promote events more widely. Not everything went smoothly. Our budget request was approved late, so we had to cancel a planned trip, and some events overlapped with exams, which hurt turnout. Next semester we want to plan the calendar earlier, survey members about what topics they want, and find a second faculty advisor. We are also thinking about a mentorship program pairing new members with seniors. Overall, we are proud of how much the club grew and excited about what comes next for everyone involved in it.

Cities around the world are experimenting with car-free zones in their downtown areas. Supporters say these zones reduce pollution, make streets safer for pedestrians, and help local shops by bringing more foot traffic. Critics worry that businesses will lose customers who drive, and that people with disabilities may find it harder to get around. Early results are mixed but promising. In several European cities, air quality improved noticeably within the first year, and surveys showed that most residents supported keeping the changes. Some shop owners reported higher sales, while others, especially those selling bulky goods, saw declines. Planners say the key is to pair car-free zones with better public transit, delivery options for businesses, and accessible transport for people who need it. Without those, they warn, the zones can feel like punishment rather than an improvement. The debate is likely to continue as more cities consider similar policies in the coming years.
